sentences.text: This animal belongs to the class Chondrichthyes, a group that includes modern sharks and rays.
Its teeth closely resemble those of the genus Bransonella, indicating a close evolutionary relationship between the two.
Despite their significance, these teeth are extremely small, measuring only 1 to 3 millimeters in height.
Tiny, claw-like denticles found on the animal are believed to have originated from a fold in the mucous membrane.
The known jawbone fragment is 37.5 cm long, though scientists estimate the complete jaw would have reached 45 cm.
Based on jaw size comparisons, this species is estimated to be the largest xenacanthid ever discovered.
The genus name honors Barbara and Alvie Claborn, who discovered and prepared the key jaw fossil.
The animal was first identified in 1970 solely from isolated teeth that were mistakenly assigned to the genus Xenacanthus.
In 2003, the species was moved to a new genus following the description of unique tooth structures and the discovery of a large jawbone at Lake Frederick.
Chemical analysis of the fossils confirms that this animal lived exclusively in freshwater environments.
Researchers later proposed that the animal was a filter feeder similar to modern basking sharks and whale sharks, consuming zooplankton.
The species was originally classified under the genus Xenacanthus as Xenacanthus luedersensis before being moved to its own genus.
The genus belongs to the parent group Bransonelliformes.
This extinct genus lived during the Early Permian and possibly the upper Pennsylvanian periods in North America.
The species lived between 303.7 and 274.4 million years ago, spanning the Gzhelian to Kungurian stages.
Fossils have been discovered in the Clear Fork, Albany, Wichita, and Dunkard Groups within the Asselian and Atinskian formations.
There is a scientific debate regarding its diet, with initial theories suggesting it swallowed prey whole, while later research suggests it was a filter feeder.
